FEATURE: Graffiti artists receive encouragement, not sanctions (2015-10-16)

facts.text: In 2005 the Taipei City Government first opened three riverside retaining walls at Dajia Yingfeng to graffiti artists.
Taipei's riverside parks now have seven official graffiti zones, run by the city's Hydraulic Engineering Office.
The seven riverside graffiti zones cover 7,630 square meters in total; the largest is 2,120 square meters and the smallest, a wall in a tunnel under a bridge, is 200 square meters.
Anyone may paint the riverside graffiti zones for free, but rude words or pictures and political slogans are removed at once.
Every four months the city paints over the riverside graffiti walls, leaving them blank for new work.
One riverside graffiti zone, under Zhongshan Bridge, was closed because it was next to the site of a historic bridge.
Painting graffiti outside the official zones breaks the Waste Disposal Act; the painter must clean it off and can be fined NT$1,200 to NT$6,000.
In 2006 Taipei's environmental protection department set up a 24-hour hotline and cash rewards for reporting graffiti.
In 2007 graffiti artists complained that the riverside walls were too far from the city center for anyone to find.
Near Ximending, a legal graffiti zone is run by a former graffiti artist, who looks at painters' earlier work before letting them paint.
On a riverside wall, a piece that took a day to paint can be covered by someone else the next day.
A Ministry of Culture official said legal graffiti parks would not end illegal graffiti but made sense for the public and for the city's appearance.
In 2015 Taipei had 10 legal graffiti zones and Taichung had seven.

notes: 多文本的兩位作者（街頭藝術家、店家）是虛構人物；城市的合法塗鴉牆以臺北市河濱塗鴉區為具體事件。
